            Sources and scope

            Scope

            The atlas draws on the six books, prologue, and appendices of The Lord of the Rings. It includes characters mentioned in retrospect and relatives or figures from earlier ages who help connect the lineages, starting with Eru and the Ainur. Legendarium marks supplementary entries. The index includes individuals and a few unnamed groups, such as the Nazgûl. Coverage follows the available indexes and genealogies. The atlas may omit unnamed minor characters and unidentified allusions.

            How to read the trees

            In the Overview map, each character has a single marker. Links cross between areas where lineages meet. Select a marker to trace recorded ancestors and descendants, including alternate parentage and missing generations. Search for a name or use the minimap to move between regions.

            In a character's tree, ancestors appear above and descendants below. Spouses appear beside each other where space allows. The profile also lists siblings, fostering relationships, and other kin. Choose Entire lineage to explore the branches. Drag to pan any map. Use the scroll wheel, a pinch gesture, or the buttons to zoom.

            Dashed lines show missing generations, fostering, or alternate versions by Tolkien. The profile explains each case. For example, Gil-galad has one parentage in the published The Silmarillion and another in a late note. Creation links connect Eru and the Ainur. Where the source records only a succession of rulers, some characters may appear without genealogical links.

            Realms and peoples

            The map covers six periods. Each marker shows a realm, region, or site associated with one or more peoples in that period. The maps cover western Middle-earth, with an inset for Aman in the First Age and Númenor in the Great Sea in the Second. Positions are relative. Borders and remote settlements in Rhûn and Harad remain uncertain.

            Places and screen adaptations

            In Places in their life, dates refer to events. The map shows the closest geographic period. A marker can represent a broader region, and a profile can list places beyond the map. Place profiles indicate when a territorial link comes from residence.

            On screen compares selected events in Peter Jackson's trilogies, The War of the Rohirrim and the first three seasons of The Rings of Power. Years in the legendarium follow the literary sources. Each adaptation follows its own sequence.

            Dates

            I, II, III, and IV indicate the Ages. CC marks Shire Reckoning, AA marks the Years of the Trees, and AV marks the Years of the Valar. Dates marked c. are approximate. Appendix C uses Shire Reckoning. Where a year can be converted, the atlas also gives its Age. Fourth Age year equivalents follow Gondor's reckoning. Shire and Gondor dates may differ at the start of the year. First Age dates and dates in the Years of the Trees can vary by manuscript and chronology.

            A dash in the date column marks a gap. Profiles distinguish death, bodily death, deposition, abdication, defeat, disappearance, and departure into the West. An event's date may establish only a time limit for the character's fate.
